Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A Saudi Arabian blogger detained in December, ostensibly because he supported reform advocates accused by the Saudi government of backing terrorism, has been released, a fellow blogger posted Saturday. Web sites like this one pushed for Fouad al-Farhan's release. Ahmed al-Omran said on his blog, saudijeans.org, and later told CNN that he was awakened by a text message from the wife of Fouad al-Farhan, saying he had been released and was at home with his family. "That's great news, and this is just how I wanted to start my morning," al-Omran wrote. He said he later spoke with al-Farhan for several minutes on the telephone. "He sounded fine; he seems to be in good spirits," al-Omran said. "He said he would have more to talk about later but not at this point. He said now he'd like to take some time to spend with his family, with his children that he hasn't seen for so long."  Watch al-Omran describe his conversation with al-Farhan » . A Web site set up to call for al-Farhan's release said, "Fouad is free. He is back home in Jeddah after 137 days in custody." The Saudi Interior Ministry said it had no immediate comment on the reports. In January, a ministry spokesman said al-Farhan was arrested December 10 "because he violated the regulations of the kingdom." But in an e-mail posted on al-Farhan's Web site after his arrest, he told friends that he faced arrest for supporting 10 reform advocates the Saudi government accused of backing terrorism. In the e-mail, al-Farhan said a senior Interior Ministry official promised that he would remain in custody for three days at most if he agreed to sign a letter of apology. "I'm not sure if I'm ready to do that," he wrote. "An apology for what? Apologizing because I said the government is [a] liar when they accused those guys of supporting terrorism?" Al-Farhan, who blogs at alfarhan.org, is one of the few Saudi Web commentators to use his own name, according to the U.S.-based Committee to Protect Journalists. In January, the Bush administration expressed its concerns to the Saudi government regarding al-Farhan's detention at "a relatively senior level," U.S. State Department spokesman Sean McCormack said. "The U.S. stands for freedom of expression," McCormack said at the time. "Wherever people are seeking to express themselves, via the Internet or via other areas, whether in Saudi Arabia or elsewhere in the world, we stand with that freedom of expression, and that was our message to the Saudi government." The American Islamic Congress, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization, launched an online letter-writing campaign aimed at freeing al-Farhan, whom it called "the godfather of Saudi blogging." "All he did was express his opinions in a very obvious way, and he didn't threaten anyone," al-Omran said. "He was advocating against violence and terrorism." Al-Omran said al-Farhan had stopped blogging for a few months in late 2006, after the Interior Ministry ordered him to take down a blog he was operating, but he began again at a new site. He said al-Farhan told him he was treated well in jail. He also called al-Farhan's release a turning point for the blogging community in Saudi Arabia. "It showed the community of bloggers in Saudi Arabia can come together and support this cause -- support his freedom of speech -- even those who didn't agree with some of the things he wrote," he said. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Mohammed Jamjoom contributed to this report.

*By CNN-style staff report*

Saudi blogger Fouad al-Farhan, one of the kingdom’s most prominent online activists, has been released after spending 137 days in custody, fellow bloggers and supporters said.

Al-Farhan, known for writing about political reform and civil rights in Saudi Arabia, was detained in December after security officials summoned him in Jeddah. His arrest drew attention from international press freedom groups and from Saudi bloggers who viewed the case as a test of the government’s tolerance for online dissent.

Fellow Saudi blogger Ahmed al-Omran welcomed the news of al-Farhan’s release, saying the blogging community was relieved after months of uncertainty over his condition and the reasons for his detention. Al-Omran, who had followed the case closely, described the release as welcome but said it also underscored the risks faced by Saudis who discuss public affairs online.

Al-Farhan’s detention was widely believed to be connected to his writings and online advocacy. Before his arrest, he had used his blog to call for reform, criticize aspects of Saudi political life and express support for jailed reformists. Supporters said he had been detained without formal charges, while Saudi authorities offered little public explanation.

In a message posted before his arrest, al-Farhan indicated he expected to be questioned by authorities and suggested it was because of his writings. The case quickly became one of the most closely watched incidents involving Internet expression in Saudi Arabia, where traditional media are tightly controlled and political criticism can carry serious consequences.

Press freedom organizations had urged Saudi authorities to either charge al-Farhan or release him. His detention also sparked concern among bloggers across the region, many of whom saw his case as part of a broader struggle over free expression in the Arab world.

Al-Farhan’s release ends more than four months of detention, but supporters said questions remain about why he was held and whether Saudi bloggers will be able to write freely about reform and human rights issues without fear of arrest.

# Saudi blogger Fouad al-Farhan released after months in detention

**RIYADH, Saudi Arabia —** Fouad al-Farhan, the prominent Saudi writer widely described by fellow activists as the “godfather of Saudi blogging,” has been released after spending more than four months in detention, according to people close to his family and human-rights advocates.

Al-Farhan, one of Saudi Arabia’s most recognizable online reform voices, had been held since December after security officials detained him in Jeddah. His case drew international attention because he was among the first Saudi bloggers known to have been arrested over online writing critical of government restrictions and in support of political prisoners.

There was no immediate detailed public explanation from Saudi authorities for his release. Rights groups had repeatedly said al-Farhan was held without formal charges and had urged the Saudi government to either charge him with a recognizable criminal offense or free him.

Before his arrest, al-Farhan sent an e-mail to friends warning that he expected to be detained.

“I have been told that there is an official order from a high-ranking official in the Ministry of Interior to investigate me,” he wrote, according to copies of the message circulated by supporters. He said he believed the move was connected to “my writings online” and his advocacy for “political prisoners” and human rights in Saudi Arabia.

In the same message, al-Farhan appeared resigned but defiant, telling friends he did not intend to stop writing about public issues. His supporters later pointed to the e-mail as evidence that authorities were targeting him for peaceful expression rather than any security offense.

## Online reform voice

Al-Farhan’s Arabic-language blog had become a meeting point for Saudis discussing political reform, civil liberties, detainees, religious influence in public life and the limits of open debate in the kingdom. At a time when blogging was emerging as a rare space for independent commentary in Saudi Arabia, activists credited him with encouraging younger writers to speak more openly.

His detention alarmed bloggers across the Arab world, many of whom launched online campaigns demanding his release. Human-rights organizations said the case underscored the Saudi government’s tight control over speech, publishing and political activism.

## U.S. criticism of speech restrictions

The United States has repeatedly criticized Saudi Arabia’s limits on freedom of expression, even as Washington maintains close security and economic ties with Riyadh.

In human-rights assessments, U.S. officials have said Saudi authorities restrict speech, the press, public assembly and political activity. The State Department has noted that criticism of the royal family, senior religious authorities or government policies can expose writers, editors and activists to harassment, censorship or detention.

U.S. criticism has also focused on the kingdom’s restrictions on independent political organizing and its controls over newspapers, broadcast media and the internet. American officials and lawmakers have urged Saudi Arabia to allow greater space for peaceful dissent and religious and political debate.

Al-Farhan’s release is likely to be welcomed by rights advocates, but they say the broader issue remains unresolved: Saudi Arabia still lacks strong legal protections for bloggers, journalists and activists who criticize state policy or call for reform.

For supporters, al-Farhan’s return home is a significant victory. But they also say his detention sent a chilling message to Saudi citizens who use the internet to discuss politics in one of the region’s most tightly controlled public spheres.
